notes: Long employment-tort appeal on unlawful means conspiracy and inducing breach; issues and authorities are fully reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Backdated employment contracts and inducing breach at software company
key_facts: IS Innovative Software sued former managing director Robert Howes for damages arising from backdated key-employee employment letters and from allegedly inducing programmers to assist his competing venture Accquiant.
Howes signed backdated letters in January 2001 believing they reflected agreed terms, but separate backdated Main Terms inserted more generous notice provisions of which he was unaware.

The judge found Howes party to an unlawful means conspiracy over the backdating but lacking intention to injure the company and that employees had not breached their contracts by giving limited technical advice while still employed.
The company appealed both findings; Howes defended in person on the second issue.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a deputy High Court judge's dismissal of tort claims in a software company dispute.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on both issues; Howes not liable for conspiracy damages or for inducing breach of contract.
enrichment.ratio: Unlawful means conspiracy requires intention to injure the claimant, not merely unlawful conduct causing loss; a conspirator is not liable for damage arising from terms he did not know of and had no reason to suspect. Employees may investigate prospective employment and give limited non-confidential technical advice without necessarily breaching exclusive-service contracts.
legal_issues: Whether oral variation gave four employees three months' notice before backdated documents were signed
Whether Howes had the requisite intention to injure for unlawful means conspiracy
Whether Howes was liable for notice terms in backdated Main Terms he never saw
Whether employees breached contracts by advising Accquiant on the IFS project
Whether the judge's credibility findings on destroyed emails could be overturned on appeal

enrichment.short_title: IS Innovative Software v Howes: conspiracy and inducement appeal dismissed
key_facts: The company appealed the dismissal of claims that Howes conspired to backdate employment documents and induced employees to assist his rival software venture Accquiant.
The Court of Appeal upheld findings that Howes lacked intention to injure over notice terms he did not know about and that employees had not breached their contracts.

Formal order: appeal dismissed with costs to the respondent subject to detailed assessment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal judgment and order on appeal from dismissal of tort claims against a former managing director.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; appellant ordered to pay respondent's costs of the appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Intention to injure is an essential element of unlawful means conspiracy; liability does not follow automatically from unlawful agreement and consequential loss. Appellate courts should not overturn primary findings of witness honesty absent plain error.

Scope of liability for backdated employment documentation

notes: Fairford anti-war protest judicial review; preventive stop held lawful but escorted return to London held unlawful detention.

enrichment.short_title: Fairford protest coaches: stop lawful, London return unlawful

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: Jane Laporte was among about 120 passengers on coaches travelling from London to join an anti-Iraq war demonstration at RAF Fairford on 22 March 2003.

Gloucestershire Police stopped and searched the coaches near Lechlade under section 60 powers, seized masks, shields and similar items, then escorted passengers back to London without allowing them to reach the protest.
Chief Superintendent Lambert reasonably feared breaches of the peace if the coaches proceeded, based on intelligence about hard-core activists including the Wombles group.
The claimant did not challenge the stop and search but contended that preventing travel and enforced return violated Articles 5, 10 and 11.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of police action preventing attendance at a demonstration and forcibly returning coach passengers to London.
enrichment.outcome: Preventing coaches proceeding to Fairford held lawful; enforced return and detention on coaches for about two and a half hours held unlawful; declaration and damages inquiry ordered.
enrichment.ratio: Police may take preventive measures short of arrest where a senior officer honestly and reasonably apprehends a real and proximate risk of breach of the peace, even if imminence is less than that required for arrest. Detention beyond brief transitory restraint to prevent an immediate breach requires arrest and prompt production before a magistrate; escorting protesters to London for hours was disproportionate and not justified under Article 5(1)(b) or (c).
legal_issues: Whether preventing coaches reaching Fairford was a lawful preventive measure
Whether escorting passengers back to London amounted to unlawful detention
Application of Article 5 to detention short of arrest after Albert v Lavin
Whether Article 5(1)(b) justified detention to secure fulfilment of an obligation
Proportionality of indiscriminate treatment of coach passengers
linked_authorities: Williamson v Chief Constable of the West Midlands Police [2003] EWCA Civ 337

confidence.notes: Facts, common law analysis, and Article 5 reasoning are detailed and the split outcome on stop versus return is explicit.

notes: White v Jones solicitor negligence appeal on failure to chase draft will; negligence and causation findings upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Solicitor not negligent for failing to chase unsigned draft will
key_facts: Mrs Atkins claimed Dunn & Baker were negligent after her father Reginald Webber received a draft will in February 1997 but never replied, died intestate in August 2000, and his estate passed to his widow and then her stepdaughter.
Webber had instructed the firm for a will giving his widow a life interest in his home and leaving the remainder to his daughter, but he did not respond to the draft letter of 25 February 1997.
The recorder found it reasonable to treat silence as a lapse of instructions and that a reminder would probably not have caused Webber to execute the will.
The claimant had a White v Jones claim as intended beneficiary.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Exeter County Court dismissal of a solicitor negligence claim by an intended beneficiary.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no negligence in failing to send a reminder and causation not established; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: A solicitor who has promptly prepared and sent a draft will in accordance with instructions does not invariably owe a duty to chase a client who fails to respond; whether a reminder is required depends on the circumstances. Where the client was meticulous, understood intestacy consequences, and gave no reply, absence of response may reasonably be treated as abandonment of the retainer, and causation may fail if a reminder would probably not have changed the outcome.
legal_issues: Whether a solicitor must follow up an unreturned draft will
Effect of client silence on continuation of the retainer
Whether failure to chase fell below the standard of a reasonably competent solicitor
Whether a reminder would probably have led to execution of the will

confidence.notes: Recorder's findings on negligence, retainer, and causation are clearly summarised and upheld on appeal.

notes: GMC professional performance suspension appeal by litigant in person; all four procedural grounds rejected.

enrichment.short_title: GMC six-month suspension appeal dismissed on all grounds

statutes_considered.title: General Medical Council (Professional Performance) Rules Order of Council 1997
General Medical Council (Constitution of Fitness to Practise Committees) (Traditional Arrangements) Rules Order of Council 2003

key_facts: Dr K Shanker appealed a General Medical Council Professional Performance Committee decision of 22 August 2003 imposing a further six-month suspension from practice.
Previous suspensions had been ordered in November 2001 and August 2002 following concerns about seriously deficient performance.

Dr Shanker argued inadequate notice, lack of jurisdiction to order further assessment, improper committee composition, and unfair reliance on Dr Norris changing his evidence after seeing an assessment report.
He appeared in person; the GMC was represented by counsel.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal against a GMC Professional Performance Committee suspension order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on all grounds; leave to appeal further refused; costs ordered against Dr Shanker.
enrichment.ratio: Adequate notice under Rule 12(3) is satisfied by proper delivery to the registered address within 28 days even if the practitioner did not personally receive it. Rule 6 disqualification applies only where a member sat on a different category of Fitness to Practise Committee, not on an earlier hearing of the same committee type. The committee was entitled to rely on a defence witness who changed his view after reading the assessment report.
legal_issues: Whether 28 days' notice of resumed GMC hearing was given
Whether the committee had power to order further assessment during suspension
Whether Professor Hatch was disqualified from sitting under Rule 6
Whether reliance on Dr Norris's revised evidence was procedurally unfair

confidence.notes: Each of the four appeal points is addressed directly; underlying clinical merits of the GMC case are not fully explored.

enrichment.short_title: Anandh estate appeal: costs follow the event
key_facts: The Court of Appeal heard submissions in writing on costs following earlier appeals in litigation involving the estate of Anandh and Barnet Primary Health Care Trust.
The court considered separate costs consequences for a repayments claim, an overpayments claim, orders of Lloyd J and Master Bowman, and an application to Chadwick LJ.

enrichment.ratio: Unless good reason appears, costs on appeal should follow the event; discrete successful and unsuccessful claims within complex healthcare funding litigation may attract separate costs orders, with assessment timing appropriate when substantial discrete applications fail.

Whether to depart from costs follow the event

notes: Costs appeal in Mark v Mark jurisdiction litigation; Hughes J's discretionary apportionment upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Mark v Mark: no interference with jurisdiction costs order
key_facts: Mr Howard appealed against Hughes J's costs order made after the judge dismissed the husband's stay application and jurisdictional challenge in divorce proceedings.
The judge ordered costs to follow the event but gave the husband set-offs for costs on the polygamy issue, wasted hearing time, and unused witness preparation.
The husband argued the wife's shifting jurisdictional case meant he should recover substantially more costs.
The Court of Appeal declined to interfere with the judge's detailed discretionary assessment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a costs order following a contested jurisdiction and stay hearing in divorce proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Application relating to costs refused; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: A trial judge who heard full argument on costs and made a nuanced order reflecting partial success, wasted costs, and issue-based set-offs is better placed than an appellate court to assess fairness; such discretion will not be disturbed without plain error.
legal_issues: Whether the judge erred in limiting the husband's costs recovery
Appropriate set-off for success on the polygamy issue
Costs consequences of belated applications and unused witness evidence
Appellate review of costs discretion in jurisdiction disputes

notes: Post-employment race discrimination jurisdiction appeal conceded after Rhys-Harper; costs split at consent stage.

enrichment.short_title: Post-employment race claim remitted after Rhys-Harper
key_facts: Mr Lawal, a former Northern Spirit employee, complained that a post-employment reference involved racial discrimination under the Race Relations Act 1976.

Employment tribunals and the EAT held they lacked jurisdiction for events after employment ended, following Adekeye v Post Office (No 2), but the House of Lords in Rhys-Harper v Relaxion Group held jurisdiction exists where discrimination arises out of the employment relationship.
Northern Spirit conceded the jurisdiction appeal in October 2003; Lawal initially resisted a consent remitter and disputed costs.
The court also addressed a earlier Recorder objection under Article 6, resolved in Lawal's favour in the House of Lords.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal hearing after House of Lords remitter on jurisdiction following conceded appeal on post-employment discrimination.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; tribunal and EAT decisions set aside; case remitted for jurisdiction and merits; costs to Lawal up to 28 October 2003, no order thereafter.
enrichment.ratio: After Rhys-Harper, employment tribunals may hear Race Relations Act claims based on post-termination acts if they arise out of or are attributable to the employment relationship. Where a respondent reasonably offers to allow an appeal after a definitive House of Lords decision, a successful appellant who unreasonably prolongs proceedings may lose costs from that point despite eventual success.
legal_issues: Tribunal jurisdiction over post-employment discriminatory references
Effect of Rhys-Harper on Adekeye v Post Office (No 2)
Appropriate form of remitter to the employment tribunal
Costs where appeal conceded after House of Lords decision
Recorder objection and Article 6 fair trial rights
linked_authorities: Rhys-Harper v Relaxing Group Plc [2003] ICR 867
Lawal v Northern Spirit Ltd [2002] EWCA Civ 1878

confidence.notes: Jurisdiction outcome follows conceded appeal and House of Lords authority; costs reasoning is fully explained.

notes: Leading overstayer divorce jurisdiction case; domicile upheld and majority refine habitual residence analysis under Article 6.

enrichment.short_title: Overstayer wife's divorce jurisdiction: domicile and habitual residence
key_facts: A Nigerian wife petitioned for divorce in England in July 2000 while an overstayer after her husband returned to Nigeria and disputed jurisdiction.
The couple had long lived in London with substantial assets; the wife's leave to remain lapsed in April 1998 when the husband failed to include her in his indefinite leave application.
Hughes J found jurisdiction on domicile of choice but held unlawful presence barred habitual residence; the husband appealed on domicile and the wife cross-appealed on habitual residence.
The Court of Appeal held an absolute public-policy bar to illegal residence was incompatible with Article 6 access to courts in this case.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal on divorce jurisdiction under section 5(2) of the 1973 Act in high-value matrimonial litigation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; jurisdiction upheld on domicile of choice; majority held overstayers may establish habitual residence where Article 6 requires, rejecting Dicey's absolute rule.
enrichment.ratio: Acquisition of domicile of choice is a neutral connecting factor, not a public-law benefit, so illegal residence does not automatically prevent domicile though it may be relevant to intention and presence. For habitual residence and jurisdiction, an absolute rule barring reliance on unlawful presence may breach Article 6 where England is the only realistic forum; illegality is a factual factor, not a jurisdictional veto.
legal_issues: Whether an overstayer can acquire an English domicile of choice
Whether unlawful residence prevents habitual residence for divorce jurisdiction
Application of Shah ex parte Nilish Shah public policy to family proceedings
Whether the husband was habitually resident in England in the relevant year
Article 6 right of access to court for financial remedy proceedings
linked_authorities: R v Barnet LBC ex p Shah [1983] 2 AC 309

confidence.notes: Substantive jurisdictional analysis is extensive with multiple concurring judgments; final order dismisses appeals but reasoning modifies habitual residence law.

notes: Historic abuse convictions at Scawby Grove upheld; committal, delay, similar-fact and summing-up grounds rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Scawby Grove care worker: conviction and 15-year sentence upheld

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: Michael Brizzalari, a residential care worker at Scawby Grove observation and assessment centre from 1983 to 1992, was convicted on multiple counts of indecent assault, rape and buggery against vulnerable female residents and a junior staff member.
Convictions followed Operation Juno investigations into abuse at Humberside local authority homes; other senior staff including the principal had already been convicted.
The trial judge refused stays for delay, severance, and challenges to similar-fact cross-admissibility; the summing-up ran to detailed written directions.
Brizzalari was sentenced to 15 years' imprisonment; he appealed conviction and sentence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) appeal against conviction and sentence after a six-week trial on historic institutional abuse.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals against conviction and sentence dismissed; convictions held safe and 15-year total sentence not manifestly excessive.
enrichment.ratio: Operation Juno was a fresh post-1997 investigation so the CPIA 1996 committal regime applied to all counts despite earlier closed police inquiries. Delay and missing documents did not make trial unfair where the judge gave adequate delay directions and identified missing material. In false-allegation multi-complainant cases, similar allegations may be cross-admissible if sufficiently connected and the jury is warned against propensity reasoning.
legal_issues: Validity of committal under CPIA 1996 after earlier 1991-92 investigations
Whether delay and missing documents warranted staying the prosecution
Admissibility of similar-fact evidence under DPP v P
Adequacy of summing-up on delay, similar facts and section 34 inferences
Whether 15 years' imprisonment was manifestly excessive
linked_authorities: R v M [2000] 1 Cr App R 49
